lead: One click on a shopping page passes through three kinds of work: the interface the user touches, the server logic that decides what to do, and the database that stores the answer. Each kind of work is a role. A front-end developer owns the first, a back-end developer the second, and a full stack developer can move across all three. MERN is one common combination, in which JavaScript runs in both the browser and the server. Job ads at Indian product companies and startups are written in exactly these words, so you need to know what each one promises.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for client, server and data tiers, 1.3 for what browsers and application servers do, and 1.4 for HTTP methods and status codes.

sections.h3: Front end, back end and the data store

blocks.text: A web system is split into tiers so each part can be built and replaced on its own. Each tier needs people who know it well, and the common job titles follow that split.

items: Front end. The code that runs in the browser: HTML for structure, CSS for appearance, JavaScript for behaviour, plus a UI framework such as React or Angular. This person also cares about accessibility (can a screen reader use the page?) and browser performance (how soon does the page become usable?).

Back end. The code that runs on the application server: the server language, URL routing, business logic, authentication, and the queries that reach the database. It answers requests; it does not draw screens.
Database. The store and its query language. This person designs the schema, writes queries and chooses indexes.

blocks.text: DevOps supports all three tiers and is sometimes counted as an extra layer of the stack. DevOps covers build, test, deploy and monitor. It is a real role in industry and is taught later (see Unit 6, Node.js, Express and Databases).

sections.h3: What the full stack developer actually does

blocks.text: A full stack developer can write the React component, add the Express route, and change the MongoDB query that feeds it. The value is not being the best at each layer. The value is that one person can carry a feature from the button to the disk and back.
A user reports that an order total is wrong. The work then goes down the request path, one layer at a time.

items: Open the browser console and check the value React received.
Open the network tab and read the JSON the API returned.
Check the server log to confirm which route ran and what it returned.
Query the database to see the stored document.
Fix the first layer where the number is already wrong, then re-check at the API boundary.

blocks.text: Small teams and startups rely on this role because one person can ship a whole feature. Large teams split it again into specialists. Do not read full stack as expert in everything; it means working knowledge across the path, with depth in one or two layers.

sections.h3: MERN: one language on both sides

blocks.text: MERN is a named stack, four technologies that fit together because all four speak JavaScript.

items: MongoDB — the database. It stores documents, which are JSON-shaped records, inside collections.
Express — the web framework on the server. It maps an HTTP method and path to a handler function.
React — the front-end library. It renders the UI from data and updates it when the data changes (see Unit 5, Front-End Frameworks: React and Angular).
Node.js — the runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, so the server code is JavaScript too.

blocks.text: Node.js is a runtime, not a framework. Express is the framework that runs on top of it.

items: The user clicks Add to cart, and a React event handler runs in the browser.
React calls fetch with method POST and path /api/cart, sending a JSON body.
Node.js accepts the connection and hands the request to Express.
Express matches the method and path to a route handler.
The handler validates the request and queries MongoDB.
MongoDB returns the matching document.
Express sends a JSON response with status 200.
React updates its state and the browser repaints the cart count.

blocks.text: Other stacks do the same work with different parts. PHP with MySQL, or Java with Spring and a relational database, are equally full stack (see Unit 4, Server-Side Scripting: PHP and Java). The tiers stay the same; only the languages change.

figure.caption: The request path of a MERN product page: React in the browser asks the Express route, which runs on Node.js and reads MongoDB. Notice that the 12 KB response is 20 products of 0.6 KB each, and that peak traffic of 8 requests per second sits well under the 40 requests per second the server can take.

spec.aria: Stack from React UI at top through Express and Node.js to MongoDB at bottom, labelled with 12 KB response, 8 requests per second peak, 40 requests per second max and 250 products.

examples.question: A MERN product page loads 20 products. Each product is sent as 0.6 KB of JSON. MongoDB holds 250 products. Express can serve up to 40 requests per second, and peak traffic is 8 requests per second. (a) Find the JSON size of the product list. (b) Find the spare capacity in requests per second and express it as a multiple of peak traffic. (c) Name the layer that owns a product document.
steps: JSON size = number of products × size per product = 20 × 0.6 KB.
20 × 0.6 = 12, so the response carries 12 KB of JSON.
As a multiple of peak: 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so the server has 4 times the peak load spare (its total capacity is 5 times peak).
Ownership: MongoDB stores the product document. Express reads it and returns JSON; React only renders what it receives.
examples.answer: The product list is 12 KB of JSON, 32 requests/s of spare capacity remain (4 times peak traffic), and MongoDB owns the product document.
examples.check:
products = 20
kb_each = 0.6
json_kb = products * kb_each
capacity = 40.0
peak = 8.0
spare = capacity - peak
multiple = spare / peak
print(json_kb)
print(spare)
print(multiple)

examples.question: A page loads 30 products, each sent as 0.8 KB of JSON. The server handles up to 50 requests per second, and peak traffic is 10 requests per second. Find the JSON size and the spare capacity as a multiple of peak.
steps: Multiple of peak = spare ÷ peak = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 times.
examples.answer: The list is 24 KB of JSON and 40 requests/s of spare capacity remain, which is 4 times peak traffic (total capacity is 5 times peak).

traps: MERN is not required for full stack work. A developer using PHP with MySQL, or Java with Spring, is just as full stack.
Node.js is a runtime, not a web framework. Express is the framework. Writing Node framework in an answer loses the mark.
MongoDB stores documents in collections. Rows and tables belong to relational databases such as MySQL.
React never talks to MongoDB directly. Every read and write crosses the HTTP API.
Full stack does not mean expert in every layer. The safe phrasing is breadth across the request path with depth in one or two layers.

quiz.q: Name the four technologies in MERN and state the job of each in one phrase.
quiz.a: MongoDB — document database. Express — server web framework and routing. React — browser UI library. Node.js — JavaScript runtime on the server.

quiz.q: Which layer owns a product document, and which layer renders it?
quiz.a: MongoDB owns and stores the document. React renders whatever the API returns for it.

quiz.q: Why is Node.js called a runtime and not a framework?
quiz.a: A runtime is the environment that executes code and provides APIs such as file system and network access. A framework supplies structure and calls your code. Express is that framework, and it runs on the Node.js runtime.

quiz.q: A page loads 30 products at 0.8 KB of JSON each. The server handles 50 requests per second, and peak traffic is 10 requests per second. Find the JSON size and the spare capacity as a multiple of peak.
quiz.a: JSON size = 30 × 0.8 = 24 KB. Spare capacity = 50 − 10 = 40 requests/s. Multiple of peak = spare ÷ peak = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 times (total capacity is 5 times peak).

quiz.q: An order total shows ₹0 in the browser, but the database holds the correct amount. Which layer do you inspect first, and why?
quiz.a: Inspect the network tab first, because it separates browser from server. If the API returned the right number, the bug is in React state or rendering. If the JSON is wrong, move to the Express handler and then to the MongoDB query. The first layer where the value is already wrong owns the bug.

quiz.q: A teammate says: we use MERN, so we are a full stack team. Is that correct?
quiz.a: Not by itself. Full stack is a role that spans front end, back end and data. MERN is one set of tools that fills those three places; PHP with MySQL or Java with Spring fill them equally.

beyond: Not for the exam. Frameworks that merge the two sides are now common: Next.js renders React on the server, and serverless functions replace a long-running Express server for small APIs. TypeScript has become the default language for new Node projects because it catches type errors before deployment. DevOps — containers, CI and CD, monitoring — is often described as an extra layer alongside front end, back end, database and the runtime. Interviews for MERN roles usually walk the whole request path rather than testing one framework. Search for React server components, Next.js API routes, and the Node.js event loop to go further.
